LESSON 37 OF 106·Operating Systems and the Command Line

Linux Permissions, Users and Groups

Read and reason about Linux permissions: owner, group and other bits, octal and symbolic modes, and why setuid, the sticky bit and shared accounts decide who can change what.

Beginner13 min
Why this matters

Linux file permissions and ownership are simple enough to reason about in full. That simplicity is the point: a reviewer can usually tell whether an access decision is correct just by looking.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Every file has an owner, a group and a set of permission bits for the owner, the group and everyone else.
  • Directory permissions mean something different from file permissions: read lists names, write creates or deletes entries, and search permits traversal.
  • Processes run with a user and a group, and may temporarily gain additional groups.
  • Special permissions such as setuid and setgid change the effective identity used for access decisions.
  • Access is decided on the path, so a directory without search permission blocks access to everything beneath it.

The background

  • The Unix permission model was designed to be understandable, with three classes and three bits rather than a growing access control list.
  • Access control lists and mandatory access control were later added for cases the simple model could not express.
  • Container platforms rely heavily on user namespaces and capabilities, which extend the model rather than replace it.
  • Modern distros ship with additional confinement features because the simple model has known gaps.

Real-world examples

  • A world-readable private key file is one of the most common and most avoidable exposures on a Linux server.
  • A service running as root does not benefit from any file permission restriction, so a single flaw has full effect.
  • A directory with write permission for a group lets any member rename or delete files beneath it, regardless of the file own permissions.

What to look for

  • Look for world-readable files that should be restricted, especially keys and configuration with secrets.
  • Check which user each service runs as, and whether it has the privileges it actually needs.
  • Review setuid and setgid bits, since they change effective identity silently.
  • Check directory permissions, because they can grant or remove access regardless of the files inside.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Linux Fundamentals Part 2

File-system interaction on an isolated Linux machine: navigating paths, creating and inspecting files, and seeing ownership and modes behave

Open TryHackMe resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Restrict sensitive files to their owning user, and verify with an unprivileged account rather than by eye.
  • Run services as dedicated unprivileged users, and use capabilities for specific privileges instead of running as root.
  • Review setuid and setgid entries, and remove any that are not clearly required.
  • Use directories to apply default permissions to new files, so correct access is inherited rather than remembered.
  • Audit with a listing of ownership and mode rather than trusting the intentions of whoever created the file.
